    (k : ℕ)

    (f : DeningerMeyerCap) {ρ : ℂ}
    (hρ0 : 0 < ρ.re) (hρ1 : ρ ≠ 1)
    (k : ℕ)
    (hζjets :

    iteratedDeriv k

by
  let U : Set ℂ := {z : ℂ | 0 < z.re} \ {1}
  have hUopen : IsOpen U :=
    (isOpen_lt
      continuous_const Complex.continuous_re).sdiff
      isClosed_singleton
  have hρU : ρ ∈ U := ⟨hρ0, hρ1⟩
  have heq :
      (fun z : ℂ =>
        deningerMeyerStrongLogMellin
          (deningerMeyerStrongLogSumLM f) z) =ᶠ[𝓝 ρ]
        fun z : ℂ => riemannZeta z * mellin f.val z := by
    filter_upwards [hUopen.mem_nhds hρU] with z hz
    simpa only [] using
      deningerMeyerStrongLogMellin_boundary_eq_zeta_mul_mellin_of_re_pos
        f hz.1 hz.2
  rw [heq.iteratedDeriv_eq k]
  have hζsmooth :
      ContDiffAt ℂ (k : WithTop ℕ∞) riemannZeta ρ :=
    (analyticOn_riemannZeta ρ hρ1).contDiffAt
  have hmellinAnalytic :
      AnalyticAt ℂ (mellin f.val) ρ := by
    apply
      DifferentiableOn.analyticAt
        (s := {z : ℂ | 0 < z.re})
    · intro z hz
      exact
        (differentiableAt_mellin_schwartzMap_of_re_pos
          f.val hz).differentiableWithinAt
    · exact
        (isOpen_lt
          continuous_const Complex.continuous_re).mem_nhds hρ0
  change
    iteratedDeriv k
      (riemannZeta * mellin f.val) ρ = 0
  rw [iteratedDeriv_mul
    hζsmooth hmellinAnalytic.contDiffAt]
  apply Finset.sum_eq_zero
  intro j hj
  have hjle : j ≤ k :=
    Nat.le_of_lt_succ (Finset.mem_range.mp hj)
  rw [hζjets j hjle]
  simp

by
  let p : ℂ → ℂ := fun z => P.eval z
  have hpAn : AnalyticOnNhd ℂ p Set.univ :=
    P.differentiable.differentiableOn.analyticOnNhd isOpen_univ
  have hpMero : Meromorphic p := fun z => (hpAn z (Set.mem_univ z)).meromorphicAt
  have hfMero : Meromorphic f := fun z => (hf z (Set.mem_univ z)).meromorphicAt
  have hpMeroOn : MeromorphicOn p Set.univ := fun z _ => hpMero z
  have hfMeroOn : MeromorphicOn f Set.univ := fun z _ => hfMero z
  have hpDiff : Differentiable ℂ p := P.differentiable
  obtain ⟨zp, hzp⟩ := hPne
  obtain ⟨zf, hzf⟩ := hfne
  have hpOrder : ∀ z, meromorphicOrderAt p z ≠ ⊤ := by
    intro z
    rw [(hpAn z (Set.mem_univ z)).meromorphicOrderAt_eq]
    have hz := GaloisForLFunctions.analyticOrderAt_ne_top_of_entire hpDiff hzp z
    simp [hz]
  have hfDiff : Differentiable ℂ f :=
    Complex.analyticOnNhd_univ_iff_differentiable.mp hf
  have hfOrder : ∀ z, meromorphicOrderAt f z ≠ ⊤ := by
    intro z
    rw [(hf z (Set.mem_univ z)).meromorphicOrderAt_eq]

prose.text:
Deninger’s program is an attempt to explain the Riemann zeta function **geometrically and cohomologically**, in the same structural way that zeta functions over finite fields are explained by étale cohomology and Frobenius.

The slogan is:

[
\boxed{\text{primes} \leftrightarrow \text{periodic orbits},
\qquad
\text{zeros} \leftrightarrow \text{eigenvalues on cohomology}.}
]

## 1. The finite-field model

Let (C) be a smooth projective curve over (\mathbb F_q). Its zeta function can be written

[
Z(C,u)
======

\exp\left(
\sum_{n\ge 1}\frac{#C(\mathbb F_{q^n})}{n}u^n
\right).
]

Étale cohomology supplies finite-dimensional spaces (H^i_{\mathrm{ét}}) on which the Frobenius map (\mathrm{Fr}_q) acts, and the zeta function becomes an alternating product of characteristic polynomials:

[
Z(C,u)
======

\prod_{i=0}^{2}
\det!\left(
1-u,\mathrm{Fr}*q
\mid H^i*{\mathrm{ét}}
\right)^{(-1)^{i+1}}.
]

In particular,

[
Z(C,u)
======

\frac{
\det(1-u,\mathrm{Fr}_q\mid H^1)
}{
\det(1-u,\mathrm{Fr}_q\mid H^0)
\det(1-u,\mathrm{Fr}_q\mid H^2)
}.
]

If the eigenvalues of Frobenius on (H^1) are (\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_{2g}), the nontrivial numerator is

[
\prod_j(1-\alpha_j u).
]

Thus the zeros of the zeta function are literally determined by the spectrum of a geometric operator.

The finite-field Riemann hypothesis says

[
|\alpha_j|=q^{1/2}.
]

Writing (u=q^{-s}), a zero satisfies (q^s=\alpha_j), so

[
\Re s=\log_q|\alpha_j|=\frac12.
]

For curves this result was originally proved by Weil; Deligne proved the corresponding purity statement for general smooth projective varieties, completing the Weil conjectures in full generality. ([arXiv][1])

## 2. Why there is no ordinary Frobenius over (\mathbb Z)

For (\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q), there is a distinguished discrete transformation:

[
x\longmapsto x^q.
]

But for (\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb Z), there is no single finite field size (q), and hence no single global Frobenius endomorphism.

Deninger’s proposal is to replace the discrete powers

[
\mathrm{Fr}_q^n
]

by a **continuous one-parameter flow**

[
\phi^t,\qquad t\in\mathbb R.
]

The flow would act on some hypothetical geometric or foliated space associated to an arithmetic scheme. The induced action on cohomology would have the form

[
\phi^{t*}=e^{t\Theta},
]

where (\Theta) is the infinitesimal generator. This (\Theta) is what is informally called the “Frobenius-flow operator.”

So the dictionary is

[
\text{finite-field Frobenius }\mathrm{Fr}_q
\quad\rightsquigarrow\quad
\text{continuous flow }\phi^t=e^{t\Theta}.
]

## 3. How the zeros would be the spectrum

For an arithmetic scheme (X), Deninger formally expects cohomology spaces

[
H^i(X)
]

carrying the operator (\Theta), such that the completed zeta function has a regularized determinant expression

[
\boxed{
\widehat{\zeta}*X(s)
\stackrel{?}{=}
\prod_i
\det*{\infty}\left(
\frac{s-\Theta}{2\pi}
\biggm|H^i(X)
\right)^{(-1)^{i+1}}.
}
]

The symbol (\det_\infty) is a zeta-regularized determinant, needed because the relevant cohomology spaces and spectra would generally be infinite-dimensional. Deninger explicitly proposed such determinant and trace formulas, with (\Theta) the infinitesimal generator of the cohomological flow. ([EMIS][2])

For (\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb Z), one informally expects only degrees (0,1,2):

[
\widehat{\zeta}(s)
\stackrel{?}{=}
\frac{
\det_\infty(s-\Theta\mid H^1)
}{
\det_\infty(s-\Theta\mid H^0)
\det_\infty(s-\Theta\mid H^2)
},
]

up to normalization factors such as (2\pi).

The intended spectral picture is

[
\operatorname{Spec}(\Theta\mid H^0)={0},
\qquad
\operatorname{Spec}(\Theta\mid H^2)={1},
]

accounting for the poles at (s=0) and (s=1) of the completed zeta function, while

[
\boxed{
\operatorname{Spec}(\Theta\mid H^1)
===================================

{\rho:\widehat{\zeta}(\rho)=0,\ \rho\text{ nontrivial}}.
}
]

Multiplicity of an eigenvalue would equal multiplicity of the corresponding zero.

Thus the claim that “the spectrum gives the zeros” is not merely metaphorical: it means that the zeta function should be the characteristic determinant of (\Theta).

## 4. Why primes become periodic orbits

The Euler product is

[
\zeta(s)
========

# \prod_p(1-p^{-s})^{-1}

\prod_p\left(1-e^{-s\log p}\right)^{-1}.
]

This looks like a dynamical zeta function in which each prime (p) corresponds to a primitive closed orbit of length

[
\boxed{\ell(p)=\log p.}
]

Its (k)-fold iterate then has length

[
k\log p,
]

which matches the prime-power terms (p^k) appearing in the logarithmic derivative

[
-\frac{\zeta'}{\zeta}(s)
========================

\sum_p\sum_{k\ge1}
(\log p)e^{-sk\log p}.
]

Deninger therefore seeks a dynamical system satisfying

[
p
\longleftrightarrow
\gamma_p,
\qquad
\ell(\gamma_p)=\log p.
]

# Deninger arithmetic cohomology for the arithmetic curve

- **ID:** `deninger-arithmetic-cohomology-construction`
- **Stage:** 1-in-progress
- **Type:** CONJECTURAL CONSTRUCTION / RH PROGRAM
- **Primary target:** `docs/Deninger program.md`
- **Rule:** construct from Deninger's rational-Witt dynamical space with the derived
  Milnor--Witt coefficient complex.  Euler--Gamma/Xi objects are comparison targets only.
- **Active concise ledger:**
  `deninger-source-native-arithmetic-cohomology-roadmap.md`.

## Scope correction

The desired object is not one analytic estimate and not a Hilbert--Pólya operator in isolation.
For \(\overline{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb Z}\), it must simultaneously provide:

1. \(K_{\mathbb R}\)-valued cohomology in degrees \(0,1,2\);
2. a closed Frobenius-flow generator \(\Theta\);
3. cup product, trace, and Poincaré duality;
4. a distributional Lefschetz formula with prime-power and archimedean local terms;
5. a regularized determinant equal to the completed zeta function;
6. an odd quaternionic Hodge star and a positive metric;
7. a source-derived comparison identifying the middle spectrum with the nontrivial Xi divisor.

CCM cyclic cohomology is frozen. It is not the arithmetic cohomology theory, it supplies none of
the missing source Hodge--Green positivity, and no further CCM work is in scope before every
Deninger gate on this card is closed. A later comparison theorem may be opened only after the
arithmetic theory and RH derivation are complete.

## Literature constraints

Deninger's properties 2.1--2.7 require:

- \(\Theta\) is a derivation of cup product;
- \(H^0=\mathbb C\) with \(\Theta=0\);
- \(H^1\) is infinite-dimensional and its generalized eigenvalues are nontrivial zeta zeros;
- \(H^2\cong\mathbb C(-1)\), so \(\Theta=1\) after trace;
- the \(H^1\times H^1\to H^2\) pairing is perfect;
- an anti-linear \(*\) on \(H^1\) satisfies \(*^2=-1\), commutes with \(\Theta\), and turns
  \(\operatorname{tr}(x\cup *y)\) into a positive scalar product.

The 2022 no-real-coefficients theorem rules out an ordinary functorial real-valued Weil theory.
Odd degree must instead carry quaternionic parity in \(K_{\mathbb R}\); degrees \(0,2\) are even.

## Active Deninger source coefficient

The active middle coefficient is no longer the entire Xi quotient described
later in this historical card.  It is Meyer's source-defined
Poisson--zeta quotient
\[
 H_\cap
 =
 \{f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R)^{\mathrm{even}}:
       f(0)=\mathcal Ff(0)=0\},
 \qquad
 M_\zeta
 =
 H_-\Big/\left\{x\mapsto\sum_{n\ge1}f(nx):f\in H_\cap\right\}.       \tag{A}
\]
The differential in `(A)` is the sum of Deninger's discrete
positive-time flow pullbacks on the canonical Hilbert--Kummer
suspension radius:
\[
 [F_nP,u]=[P,nu]=\phi^{\log n}[P,u].
\]
It is defined without a zero divisor.  Poisson summation supplies its
real-place gluing; its Euler factorization supplies the finite-prime
maps.

Joining `(A)` to the proved strict Milnor--Arakelov endpoint gives a
source-defined three-term complex with
\[
 H^0=\mathbb C,\qquad H^1=M_\zeta,\qquad H^2=\mathbb C(-1).
\]
The abstract assembly and its concrete finite-plus-real Arakelov
endpoint are now formalized unconditionally in Lean:
`DeningerArithmeticPoissonZetaAssembly.lean` proves the quotient
calculation, while
`DeningerArithmeticArakelovPoissonComplex.lean` proves the concrete
\(H^0/H^1/H^2\) equivalences and endpoint cup pairing.
Meyer's theorems give the exact zero spectrum with multiplicity and the
prime-plus-archimedean Weil character.  Deninger's regularized-product
theorem gives the completed-zeta determinant.  Paugam gives the
unconditional alternating spectral pairing and, through upper/lower
sign--conjugation, the odd spectral \(K_{\mathbb R}\)-operator with
square \(-1\).  Positivity of the resulting sesquilinear form remains
the RH-bearing gate.  These statements are
recorded, with topology caveats, in
`DAC_POISSON_ZETA_THREE_TERM_COHOMOLOGY`.

The two exact open source gates are:

1. `DAC_DENINGER_POISSON_RELEVANT_COMPLEX_COMPARISON`: construct the
   logarithmic Schwartz collar on Deninger's rational-Witt suspension

2. Construct a positive flow-natural Hodge polarization on the resulting

All Xi-divisor, Euler--Gamma, and Hilbert completions below are frozen

# Critical radial \(L^2\) quotient as arithmetic Hodge cohomology

- **ID:** `deninger-critical-radial-l2-hodge-quotient`
- **Stage:** 5-failed
- **Type:** NO-GO WITH POSITIVE SURVIVOR
- **Label:** `DAC_CRITICAL_RADIAL_L2_POISSON_QUOTIENT_NO_GO`
- **Parent:** `deninger-poisson-hodge-polarization`
- **Statement:** the local Hermitian radial-line metric is the correct
  critical measure, but completing Meyer's Poisson complex in that
  scalar \(L^2\) space makes the Poisson range dense and erases reduced
  middle cohomology.

## Candidate

The Hermitian radial-line theorem gives
\[
 L^2_{1/2}
 =
 L^2(\mathbb R_{>0},x\,d^\times x)
 =
 L^2(\mathbb R_{>0},dx).                                         \tag{1}
\]
The centered dilation flow is unitary on `(1)`, and the local
degree-one Hodge star is positive.  The tempting construction is
\[
 \overline{H_-}^{\,L^2_{1/2}}
 \Big/
 \overline{Z(H_\cap)}^{\,L^2_{1/2}}.                             \tag{2}
\]

## Density theorem

`[PROVED HERE] [DAC_CRITICAL_RADIAL_L2_POISSON_QUOTIENT_NO_GO]`

\[
 \overline{Z(H_\cap)}^{\,L^2(\mathbb R_{>0},dx)}
 =
 L^2(\mathbb R_{>0},dx).                                         \tag{3}
\]
Consequently the reduced Hilbert cohomology in `(2)` is zero.

### Proof

First \(H_\cap\) is dense in \(L^2(\mathbb R_{>0},dx)\).
Compactly supported smooth functions away from zero are dense.  After
even extension, the condition \(f(0)=0\) already holds.  The remaining
condition
\[
 \widehat f(0)=\int_{\mathbb R}f(x)\,dx=0
\]
can be imposed with arbitrarily small \(L^2\) error: subtract a smooth
even plateau of integral \(\int f\), supported on an interval of
length \(L\) far from the original support.  Its amplitude is
\(O(L^{-1})\), hence its \(L^2\) norm is \(O(L^{-1/2})\).

The critical Mellin transform is unitary, up to normalization,
\[
 \mathcal M_{1/2}:
 L^2(\mathbb R_{>0},dx)
 \longrightarrow L^2(\mathbb R,dt).                              \tag{4}
\]
On \(H_\cap\),
\[
 \mathcal M_{1/2}(Zf)(t)
 =
 \zeta\!\left(\frac12+it\right)
 \mathcal M_{1/2}f(t).                                           \tag{5}
\]
The meromorphic function \(\zeta\) is not identically zero, so its
zeros on the critical line form a measure-zero discrete set.

If \(g\) is orthogonal to the range in `(5)`, then
\[
 \int_{\mathbb R}
 \zeta\!\left(\frac12+it\right)
 \mathcal M_{1/2}f(t)\overline{g(t)}\,dt=0
 \qquad(f\in H_\cap).
\]
Density of the Mellin core implies
\[
 \overline{\zeta(1/2+it)}\,g(t)=0
\quad\text{a.e.}
\]
Since the multiplier is nonzero almost everywhere, \(g=0\).
Thus the orthogonal complement of \(Z(H_\cap)\) is zero, proving
`(3)`.

## Why local Hodge positivity does not descend

The local star commutes with the differential on the test core, but
Hilbert harmonic cohomology represents the quotient by the
**closure** of the differential range.  Equation `(3)` makes that
harmonic space zero.  Therefore:

- local Kähler positivity is genuine;
- the critical measure is forced and correct;
- scalar Hilbert completion before nuclear cohomology is wrong.

This is the exact distinction between a positive source metric and a
faithful positive metric on \(M_\zeta\).

## Strongest positive survivor

1. Form the strict nuclear quotient
   \(M_\zeta=H_-/Z(H_\cap)\) first.
2. Retain the Gelfand rigging
   \[
   H_{\mathrm{test}}\subset H_{\mathrm{Hilb}}
   \subset H_{\mathrm{test}}'
   \]
   without identifying nuclear cohomology with the reduced scalar
   Hilbert quotient.
3. A successful arithmetic leaf complex must contain additional
   source coefficient/transverse data whose closed reduced harmonic
   image maps faithfully into \(M_\zeta'\).  The scalar radial line
   alone cannot do this.
4. Cup-isometric faithfulness of that map is the RH-bearing theorem;
   it cannot be inferred from local star positivity.

## No-go closure

- **Killed representation:** scalar critical-\(L^2\) completion of
  the Poisson cokernel.
- **Killing mechanism:** Mellin multiplication by a nonzero-a.e.
  zeta multiplier has dense range.
- **Positive invariant:** exact forced critical measure and local
  weight-one Hodge star survive as one channel of a larger rigged
  coefficient.
- **Paper status:** dependency-closed proof above.
- **Lean status:** abstract dense-multiplier formalization pending a
  low-load window.

Over a finite field, the zeta function is rational, and each (H^i) is finite-dimensional. Its numerator and denominator therefore contain only finitely many Frobenius eigenvalues.

The Riemann zeta function has infinitely many nontrivial zeros. Therefore, if all those zeros are the spectrum of (\Theta\mid H^1), then (H^1) must be infinite-dimensional.

### Splitting statements into different characteristic

Statements to split a proof by characteristic. There are 3 theorems here that are very
similar. They only differ in the assumptions we can make on the positive characteristic
case:
Generally we need to consider all `p ≠ 0`, but if `R` is a local ring, we can assume
that `p` is a prime power. And if `R` is a domain, we can even assume that `p` is prime.

section MainStatements

variable {P : Prop}

/-- Split a `Prop` in characteristic zero into equal and mixed characteristic. -/
theorem split_equalCharZero_mixedCharZero [CharZero R] (h_equal : Algebra ℚ R → P)
    (h_mixed : ∀ p : ℕ, Nat.Prime p → MixedCharZero R p → P) : P := by
  by_cases h : ∃ p > 0, MixedCharZero R p
  · rcases h with ⟨p, ⟨H, hp⟩⟩
    rw [← MixedCharZero.reduce_to_p_prime] at h_mixed
    exact h_mixed p H hp
  · apply h_equal
    rw [← isEmpty_algebraRat_iff_mixedCharZero, not_isEmpty_iff] at h
    exact h.some

/--
Split any `Prop` over `R` into the three cases:
- positive characteristic.
- equal characteristic zero.
- mixed characteristic `(0, p)`.
-/
theorem split_by_characteristic (h_pos : ∀ p : ℕ, p ≠ 0 → CharP R p → P)
    (h_equal : Algebra ℚ R → P)
    (h_mixed : ∀ p : ℕ, Nat.Prime p → MixedCharZero R p → P) : P := by
  cases CharP.exists R with
  | intro p p_charP =>
    by_cases h : p = 0
    · rw [h] at p_charP
      haveI h0 : CharZero R := CharP.charP_to_charZero R
      exact split_equalCharZero_mixedCharZero R h_equal h_mixed
    · exact h_pos p h p_charP

/--
In an `IsDomain R`, split any `Prop` over `R` into the three cases:
- *prime* characteristic.
- equal characteristic zero.
- mixed characteristic `(0, p)`.
-/
theorem split_by_characteristic_domain [IsDomain R]
    (h_pos : ∀ p : ℕ, Nat.Prime p → CharP R p → P)
    (h_equal : Algebra ℚ R → P) (h_mixed : ∀ p : ℕ, Nat.Prime p → MixedCharZero R p → P) : P := by
  refine split_by_characteristic R ?_ h_equal h_mixed
  intro p p_pos p_char
  have p_prime : Nat.Prime p := or_iff_not_imp_right.mp (CharP.char_is_prime_or_zero R p) p_pos
  exact h_pos p p_prime p_char

/--
In a local ring `R`, split any predicate over `R` into the three cases:
- *prime power* characteristic.
- equal characteristic zero.
- mixed characteristic `(0, p)`.
-/
theorem split_by_characteristic_localRing [IsLocalRing R]
    (h_pos : ∀ p : ℕ, IsPrimePow p → CharP R p → P) (h_equal : Algebra ℚ R → P)
    (h_mixed : ∀ p : ℕ, Nat.Prime p → MixedCharZero R p → P) : P := by
  refine split_by_characteristic R ?_ h_equal h_mixed
  intro p p_pos p_char
  have p_ppow : IsPrimePow (p : ℕ) := or_iff_not_imp_left.mp (charP_zero_or_prime_power R p) p_pos
  exact h_pos p p_ppow p_char

/-!
# Equal and mixed characteristic

In commutative algebra, some statements are simpler when working over a `ℚ`-algebra `R`, in which
case one also says that the ring has "equal characteristic zero". A ring that is not a
`ℚ`-algebra has either positive characteristic or there exists a prime ideal `I ⊂ R` such that
the quotient `R ⧸ I` has positive characteristic `p > 0`. In this case one speaks of
"mixed characteristic `(0, p)`", where `p` is only unique if `R` is local.

Examples of mixed characteristic rings are `ℤ` or the `p`-adic integers/numbers.

This file provides the main theorem `split_by_characteristic` that splits any proposition `P` into
the following three cases:

1) Positive characteristic: `CharP R p` (where `p ≠ 0`)
2) Equal characteristic zero: `Algebra ℚ R`
3) Mixed characteristic: `MixedCharZero R p` (where `p` is prime)

## Main definitions

- `MixedCharZero` : A ring has mixed characteristic `(0, p)` if it has characteristic zero
  and there exists an ideal such that the quotient `R ⧸ I` has characteristic `p`.

## Main results

- `split_equalCharZero_mixedCharZero` : Split a statement into equal/mixed characteristic zero.

This main theorem has the following three corollaries which include the positive
characteristic case for convenience:

- `split_by_characteristic` : Generally consider positive char `p ≠ 0`.
- `split_by_characteristic_domain` : In a domain we can assume that `p` is prime.
- `split_by_characteristic_localRing` : In a local ring we can assume that `p` is a prime power.

## Implementation Notes

We use the terms `EqualCharZero` and `AlgebraRat` despite there not being any such definitions
in mathlib.
The former refers to the statement `∀ I : Ideal R, I ≠ ⊤ → CharZero (R ⧸ I)`, the latter
refers to the existence of an instance `[Algebra ℚ R]`. The two are shown to be
equivalent conditions.

## TODO

- Relate mixed characteristic in a local ring to p-adic numbers [NumberTheory.PAdics].
-/

public section

/-!
### Mixed characteristic
-/

/--
A ring of characteristic zero is of "mixed characteristic `(0, p)`" if there exists an ideal
such that the quotient `R ⧸ I` has characteristic `p`.

**Remark:** For `p = 0`, `MixedChar R 0` is a meaningless definition (i.e. satisfied by any ring)
as `R ⧸ ⊥ ≅ R` has by definition always characteristic zero.
One could require `(I ≠ ⊥)` in the definition, but then `MixedChar R 0` would mean something
like `ℤ`-algebra of extension degree `≥ 1` and would be completely independent from
whether something is a `ℚ`-algebra or not (e.g. `ℚ[X]` would satisfy it but `ℚ` wouldn't).
-/
class MixedCharZero (p : ℕ) : Prop where
  [toCharZero : CharZero R]
  charP_quotient : ∃ I : Ideal R, I ≠ ⊤ ∧ CharP (R ⧸ I) p

namespace MixedCharZero

/--
Reduction to `p` prime: When proving any statement `P` about mixed characteristic rings we
can always assume that `p` is prime.
-/
lemma reduce_to_p_prime {P : Prop} :
    (∀ p > 0, MixedCharZero R p → P) ↔ ∀ p : ℕ, p.Prime → MixedCharZero R p → P := by
  constructor
  · intro h q q_prime q_mixedChar
    exact h q (Nat.Prime.pos q_prime) q_mixedChar
  · intro h q q_pos q_mixedChar
    rcases q_mixedChar.charP_quotient with ⟨I, hI_ne_top, _⟩
    -- Krull's Thm: There exists a prime ideal `P` such that `I ≤ P`
    rcases Ideal.exists_le_maximal I hI_ne_top with ⟨M, hM_max, h_IM⟩
    let r := ringChar (R ⧸ M)
    have r_pos : r ≠ 0 := by
      have q_zero :=
        congr_arg (Ideal.Quotient.factor h_IM) (CharP.cast_eq_zero (R ⧸ I) q)
      simp only [map_natCast, map_zero] at q_zero
      apply ne_zero_of_dvd_ne_zero (ne_of_gt q_pos)
      exact (CharP.cast_eq_zero_iff (R ⧸ M) r q).mp q_zero
    have r_prime : Nat.Prime r :=
      or_iff_not_imp_right.1 (CharP.char_is_prime_or_zero (R ⧸ M) r) r_pos
    apply h r r_prime
    have : CharZero R := q_mixedChar.toCharZero
    exact ⟨⟨M, hM_max.ne_top, ringChar.of_eq rfl⟩⟩

/--
Reduction to `I` prime ideal: When proving statements about mixed characteristic rings,
after we reduced to `p` prime, we can assume that the ideal `I` in the definition is maximal.
-/
lemma reduce_to_maximal_ideal {p : ℕ} (hp : Nat.Prime p) :
    (∃ I : Ideal R, I ≠ ⊤ ∧ CharP (R ⧸ I) p) ↔ ∃ I : Ideal R, I.IsMaximal ∧ CharP (R ⧸ I) p := by
  constructor
  · intro g
    rcases g with ⟨I, ⟨hI_not_top, _⟩⟩
    -- Krull's Thm: There exists a prime ideal `M` such that `I ≤ M`.
    rcases Ideal.exists_le_maximal I hI_not_top with ⟨M, ⟨hM_max, hM_ge⟩⟩
    use M
    constructor
    · exact hM_max
